t.1.180.2: Passing over us and treating us, who have gathered here, as no more than straw, this man wishes to give Draupadī, the best of women, to a brahmin.
t.1.180.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: He wishes to give the maiden to that great-souled brahmin, and at this anger arose among the kings, who looked at one another from close by.
t.1.180.4: Let us kill this evil-mannered enemy of kings together with his son! For he summoned all the lords of men, honored them, and feasted them handsomely, and then afterward he insults them.
t.1.180.3: Let us kill this evil-minded man who holds us in contempt. For by his qualities he deserves neither honor nor the deference due to elders.
t.1.180.5: In this assembly of kings, which is like a gathering of the gods, has he truly not seen even a single king who is a fitting match?
t.1.180.6: Brahmins have no right with regard to the choosing of a bride; the self-choice is for kṣatriyas, so goes this well-known tradition.
t.1.180.8: Even if this brāhmaṇa has done this thing displeasing to the lords of kings, whether out of childishness or out of greed, he is by no means to be slain.
t.1.180.7: Or else, if this maiden does not wish to take anyone here as her husband, let us kings cast her into the fire and go back to our kingdoms.
t.1.180.9: For our kingdom, our life, and our riches, our sons and grandsons, and whatever other wealth we possess, all exist for the sake of the brahmins.
t.1.180.11: Having spoken thus, those tigers among kings, elated, their arms like iron clubs, rushed together upon Drupada with their weapons, eager to seize him.
t.1.180.10: This is done from fear of dishonour and to protect our own dharma, and so that other svayaṃvaras may not come to such an end.
t.1.180.12: Seeing those enraged kings rushing at him with their quivers in hand, Drupada, out of terror, went to the brahmins for refuge.
t.1.180.13: But as they came rushing on with force like elephants in rut, the two mighty sons of Pāṇḍu, tamers of their foes, went forth to meet them.
t.1.180.15: Then Bhīma, of wondrous valor and deeds, mighty, with strength equal to the thunderbolt, the peerless hero, uprooted a tree with his two arms and stripped it of its leaves, like a lord of elephants.
t.1.180.14: Then those kings sprang up with weapons raised, their palm-guards and finger-guards bound on, eager to slay the two sons of the Kuru king, Arjuna and Bhīmasena, and assailing them in fury.
t.1.180.16: Taking up that tree, the crusher of foes, Pārtha of broad and long arms, stood beside Pārtha, the bull among men, like a staff-bearer holding his fierce staff beside the king of the ancestors.
t.1.180.18: He who strides like a rutting bull and draws the great bow, tall as a palm tree, that is Arjuna, there is no doubt about it, O Saṃkarṣaṇa, as surely as I am Vāsudeva.
t.1.180.17: Seeing that deed of the brother, Dāmodara, the victorious one of superhuman understanding and inconceivable deeds, spoke these words to his brother Halāyudha of fierce valor.
t.1.180.20: He who went out in front, with long eyes like lotus petals, slender, moving with the gait of a great lion, modest, fair-skinned, with a long, bright and handsome nose, that one, Acyuta, is the King of Dharma.
t.1.180.19: He who has violently uprooted a tree and suddenly turned back to face the kings in their hostility is Vṛkodara; no other mortal on earth could accomplish this here today.
t.1.180.21: Those two who look like two youthful Kārttikeyas are, I surmise, the twin sons of the Aśvins. For I have heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu and Pṛthā escaped from that burning of the lac house.
t.1.180.22: Halāyudha, shining like a spotless cloud, spoke gladly to his younger brother: "I am pleased, for by good fortune our father's sister Pṛthā has escaped, together with the foremost of the Kauravas."
